title: Intel Foundry: AI performance now depends on the whole system - Semiwiki
gist: Summarizing Intel Foundry's Lalitha Immaneni, the author argues AI hardware gains now require co-designing silicon, chiplets, packaging, boards and power/thermal as one system, evaluated early. Success depends on accurate modeling and a chiplet ecosystem with compatible, validated components.

insights.claim: AI workloads are exposing the limits of improving computing performance by adding more capable circuitry to a piece of silicon, because data movement, sustained power and cooling become binding constraints.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Performance gains shift from transistor scaling toward packaging, memory and thermal capability; watch suppliers of those layers.
insights.locator: For decades, chipmakers improved computing performance

insights.claim: Intel Foundry's Lalitha Immaneni argues the next performance gains will come from designing silicon, packaging, circuit boards and the wider platform as one system, a view the author fully endorses.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Signals Intel Foundry is positioning on system-level co-design rather than process leadership alone.

insights.claim: A fast processor cannot deliver its full benefit if memory cannot feed it quickly enough or if heat forces it to slow down.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Bandwidth and thermal limits cap AI accelerator value, favoring memory and cooling beneficiaries.
insights.locator: For decades, chipmakers improved computing performance

insights.claim: Bottom line: more processing circuitry alone cannot solve limits in bandwidth, energy use and heat, so co-designing the whole system could yield faster, more efficient products and fewer late redesigns.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Frames the investable shift to system-level optimization in AI hardware.

insights.claim: The package, once chiefly a way to protect a finished chip and connect it to a board, now helps determine how processors communicate with memory, how power reaches them and how heat escapes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Packaging captures more value and strategic importance in AI supply chains.
insights.locator: Advanced packaging is central to that approach

insights.claim: Splitting a large design into chiplets lets each function use the manufacturing process best suited to it and allows reuse of existing components, but raises questions about function placement, interconnect and the power, space and speed cost of those connections.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Chiplet economics hinge on interconnect cost; evaluate vendors on integration tooling.
insights.locator: One way to build such systems is to divide a large design

insights.claim: If chiplets from different suppliers are to combine easily, compatible interfaces, reliable design information and validated components are essential; otherwise each new combination risks becoming a costly custom project.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A multi-vendor chiplet ecosystem needs standards and validation; absence keeps costs high and favors integrated players.
insights.locator: Connections between chiplets are a case in point

insights.claim: AI systems can run near peak activity for long periods, creating concentrated hot spots, and chiplet placement, surrounding materials and the power delivery path through board, package and silicon limit sustainable performance.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Thermal and power-delivery solutions are first-order determinants of AI system performance.
insights.quote: These are architectural choices, not finishing touches.
insights.locator: Heat and power add further constraints

insights.claim: Tightly integrated systems force chip, package and board teams to compare options and resolve conflicts throughout development rather than passing designs sequentially, and better simulation, experimentally checked models and digital representations could help predict problems before building hardware.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Beneficiaries may include simulation and EDA toolmakers enabling early cross-domain evaluation.
insights.locator: That changes how engineers must work together

insights.claim: Finding a problem while exploring designs is far less disruptive than finding it after detailed layouts or physical prototypes are complete, so Immaneni calls for evaluating chiplet partitioning, process choice, routing, memory integration and temperature, power, yield and cost effects early.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Early-stage pathfinding capability is a differentiator for foundry and packaging offerings.
insights.locator: Immaneni calls for that evaluation to begin early

insights.claim: The system-level challenge extends beyond Intel Foundry: foundries, packaging specialists, software toolmakers, memory suppliers and customers all need ways to exchange trustworthy design information, and the approach will succeed only if interactions can be modeled accurately and chiplets made practical to combine at scale.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Execution risk sits in modeling accuracy and ecosystem interoperability, not just Intel's technology.
insights.locator: The broader challenge, however, reaches beyond any one supplier
